essence.one_sentence: Two colors mixed at a ratio give different middles depending on whether the math averages encoded numbers, averages light, or interpolates perceived lightness, and that middle is the thing a person judges.
essence.summary: Two colors, one ratio, a chosen mix model, a glyph or block picture of the mix, and a readable hex value that repaints on each key.

formula.full: two colors + one ratio + a mix model + glyph shading or block swatch + hex readout + repaint on each key
formula.essential: a ratio between two colors, drawn as a swatch with its hex value and moved by a pair of keys: one combination among several, the other kinds are in angles

roles.mix model: what the in-between colors look like
roles.block swatch: the hue as a solid fill
roles.hex readout: the exact value a person can copy and check
roles.repaint on key: feedback that makes the mix feel live

angles.text: A simple interactive ASCII color-mixing program on one terminal screen: two color chips, a bar showing the ratio between them, and a large ASCII swatch of the mix with its hex value. Arrow keys move the ratio and the screen repaints on each press.

The mix fills the screen as a field of ASCII characters from sparse to dense: density carries brightness, the glyph color carries hue, and the hex value sits underneath. Keys move the ratio and the field re-shades on each press.

Two block-swatch columns of the same pair, one per mixing model (channel mean and linear light), each labelled with its value in ASCII. One ratio control moves both columns at once, so the difference between the models shows as the ratio changes.
A prompt line under a live ASCII swatch. A person types a ratio or a color and presses Enter, and the swatch and its value update at once; the arrow keys step the same ratio live between entries.

A simple engine built from a pure function that takes two colors and a ratio and returns one color, with a thin interactive loop around it. The picture is a labelled ASCII cell with its hex value printed on the mix, and a test calls the function directly.
A row of block cells running from the first color to the second, twenty steps wide, with the chosen step marked. A swatch and a hex value sit beside the row, and the keys step along it.

glyph shading: the picture reads at a glance

code.text: Brief for a coding agent building a two-color mixer. Options side by side, not a spec. Language and platform: a single Python 3 standard-library file is one option. Mix: a pure function mix(color_a, color_b, ratio) returning one RGB triple. Model options: channel mean (one line, dim midpoints), linear light (decode, average, encode; brighter midpoints, about ten lines), paint-like multiply (black from bright pairs), CIELAB (about 40 to 60 lines of conversion). The ratio t from 0 to 1 blends as (1 - t) * A + t * B in the chosen space; step sizes of 1, 5 or 10 percent are options. State: the two colors, the ratio and the selected index; the current mix is derived from them on each change, so the swatch and the readout come from one source. Picture: a shading ramp (sparse to dense glyphs, luminance taken in linear light, hue as the foreground color), a block swatch (full block or spaces on a background), or a labelled cell (hex printed on the mix, black or white by luminance). Value: #RRGGBB and decimal R G B; the nearest of the 16 ANSI names as an approximate extra. Color output: truecolor when COLORTERM says so, 256 when TERM ends in 256color, otherwise the 16 named colors, stepping down. Starting pair, color entry and key set: the options in opt-start-colors, opt-color-entry and opt-key-map, side by side. Input: arrow or letter keys move the ratio in steps, clamped at the ends, wrapped or bounced; a bad entry prints a one-line message and keeps the old value. Size: the floors in opt-min-size, or a compact layout below them. Exit: the quit key and Ctrl-C restore the terminal; a resize triggers one redraw at the new size; piped output prints one plain value with no escape codes.

ak-color-mixing-grading.excluded_sense: photo or video colour grading (channel mixer, colour balance sliders, LUTs)
ak-color-mixing-grading.instead: the mix of two terminal colours in one cell, shown as a value and a swatch

ak-engine-game.excluded_sense: game or 3D rendering engine (scene graph, physics, frame budget)
ak-engine-game.instead: a small program with a loop and state, with a mixing function inside it

ak-noise-robust.text: Filler for a small program; it says nothing about the mixer.

ak-noise-stunning.text: Empty intensifier; the swatch and its value carry the claim.

ak-worn-input-crash.instead: a one-line message, the current mix kept on screen; Ctrl+C restores the cursor and colors
ak-worn-input-crash.text: Hex or number parsing is unguarded, so a typo raises a traceback and can leave the terminal in a bad state.

ak-worn-fixed-width.instead: the swatch and readout reflow to the current terminal size on each redraw
ak-worn-fixed-width.text: Width and height are hardcoded, so a resize wraps or tears the screen.

ak-full-block-swatch.instead: ASCII glyphs from a density ramp, or background-colored spaces with the mix as the cell color

chk-two-colors-mix.text: Does the mix of red and blue at a ratio of 0.5 come out as (128, 0, 128) under the channel mean, or as (188, 0, 188) under linear light, and does the program name the model it uses?

test.spec: Mix 255,0,0 with 0,0,255 at 0.5. The channel mean gives 128,0,128 (ev-red-blue-channel-mean at t 0.5); linear light gives 188,0,188 (ev-red-blue-linear-light at t 0.5). Either value fits a match, provided the model is named on screen or in the readout.

chk-ascii-picture.text: Is the mix drawn as a field of characters or colored cells, not only as a line of text?

test.spec: The mixed color fills a field of glyphs or block cells on screen, and the field changes when the ratio moves.

chk-simple-size.text: Do the colors, the mix and its value fit one screen, with one source file and one ratio control?

test.spec: One source file; one ratio control; the colors, the mix and its value fit on one screen at the terminal's current size.

chk-start-screen.text: Does the first screen show both starting colors, the ratio, the swatch and a value?

spec: Start the program with the starting pair set under opt-start-colors
Confirm the first screen shows both colors, the ratio, the swatch and a hex value

chk-ratio-changes-color.text: When the ratio changes, do the swatch and the value change with it?

spec: Start the program
Press the ratio-up key from the key set chosen under opt-key-map, once
Confirm the swatch color and the value readout both change
Press the ratio-down key back
Confirm the color returns to its starting value

chk-quit-clean.text: Does quitting with the quit key or Ctrl-C leave the terminal usable?

spec: Start the program
Press the quit key from opt-key-map, or Ctrl-C
Confirm the process exits within about a second
Confirm the shell prompt is normal and typed text echoes

chk-resize.text: Does a terminal resize redraw at the new size without a crash?

spec: Start the program in a narrow window
Resize the window wider, then narrower
Confirm no traceback and the screen repaints at the new size

chk-min-size.text: Below the size floor, does the screen say what size it needs instead of drawing a broken layout?

spec: Start the program in a window smaller than the floor chosen under opt-min-size
Confirm one line names the size needed, or a compact layout appears
Resize to the floor or above and confirm the full screen returns

chk-invalid-input.text: Does a bad entry keep the old ratio and color, with a one-line message?

spec: Enter text where a ratio is expected, or a bad hex in the color entry set under opt-color-entry
Confirm a one-line message appears
Confirm the ratio and the color are unchanged

chk-readable-value.text: Can a person read the mixed color's value as hex or RGB, and copy it?

spec: Mix two colors
Confirm the readout shows a hex or RGB value
Change the ratio and confirm the value changes

chk-piped-output.text: Does piped output stay free of escape codes?

spec: If the program has a one-shot or piped mode, run it with stdout sent to a file
Confirm the file holds no ESC characters

req-engine.anchor: a simple interactive ascii color mixing engine
req-engine.text: The user asks for an engine that mixes colors.

req-interactive.text: The user interacts with it while it runs.

req-simple.text: The user asks for something simple; the size word bounds the build.

color_principles._about: Discipline primer for color mixing and terminal UI. Facets, not a rulebook: the mixing models and their known results, what each reading of 'mix' does, and the mistakes tools commonly make.

cp-mixing-models.text: Light adds: overlapping lights sum their channels and get brighter. Paint subtracts: each pigment absorbs more light, so the mix gets darker and duller.
behaviors: Full red, green and blue light overlapped gives white
Two paints mixed give a darker color than either input
An RGB average of two paints matches neither model
cp-mixing-models.principle: Light sources sum; pigments multiply their absorption.
signals: darker and less saturated with each added paint

cp-linear-light.term: averaging in sRGB vs linear light
cp-linear-light.text: sRGB values are gamma-encoded, so averaging them directly is not averaging light. Decode to linear, mix, then encode back.
behaviors: The page's worked example: linear average 0.606 re-encodes to about 204 of 255, where a direct average of 127 and 255 gives 191 (worked from the page's numbers)
Blending in gamma space makes the middle of a gradient too dark
cp-linear-light.principle: Light adds in linear space, so the physically right average is taken there.
signals: muddy midpoint darker than both ends
dark seam where two colors meet

cp-lab.text: Lab separates lightness (L*) from two color axes and was built to be perceptually uniform, though only approximately.
behaviors: L* closely tracks perceived lightness, so steps in L* look steadier than steps in RGB
Lab is less uniform in the color axes, so use it for lightness and small differences
cp-lab.principle: Interpolate where equal numeric steps should look like equal perceived steps; expect approximations.
signals: blue hues drifting in a gradient

cp-hsl.text: HSL is easy to reason about by hand, but its lightness is not perceptually uniform: equal steps in L look unequal across hues. Basis: search-result snippets, not fetched pages.
behaviors: Equal HSL lightness does not mean equal brightness for yellow and blue
Good for picking a hue, weak for a true perceptual midpoint
cp-hsl.principle: HSL is a convenient UI space, not a perceptual one.
signals: yellows looking lighter than blues at the same L

cp-text-ui.term: text UI conventions (keys, Ctrl-C, pipes, color off)
cp-text-ui.text: Interactive terminal programs exit promptly on Ctrl-C, turn color off when output is not a terminal, and skip animation and prompts when not on a TTY.
properties: color off when not a TTY
behaviors: Piping the mixer's output should print plain values with no escape codes
A hang on input should still stop on Ctrl-C
cp-text-ui.principle: A terminal tool is a good citizen: it stops on Ctrl-C and stays readable when piped.

cp-mistakes.term: common mistakes in terminal color tools
cp-mistakes.text: Typical failures: muddy midpoints from gamma-space averaging, unreadable labels on a mixed background, and colors that vanish on 16-color terminals.
behaviors: A label drawn in one fixed color disappears when the mix is near that color
A hex readout is what a person can copy and check
cp-mistakes.principle: Check the mix in linear light, the label against its background, and the output in a 16-color terminal.
signals: all colors look the same in a basic terminal

cp-terminal-color.text: Colors arrive as named ANSI colors, a 256-entry palette, or 24-bit RGB, all set with SGR escape codes. Support varies, so a tool should fall back from truecolor toward named colors.
behaviors: Many terminals show bold as the brighter version of a named color
The semicolon-based RGB form is the most widely supported truecolor syntax
Truecolor values need a terminal that accepts 38;2, or they show as the wrong color
Each 24-bit escape sets one exact RGB value, so a mixed color prints without palette rounding
cp-terminal-color.principle: Degrade gracefully: truecolor, then 256, then the 16 named colors.
signals: colors look washed out or shifted on a 16-color terminal

terminal_rendering._about: Reference values for the 16 ANSI terminal colors. One terminal's palette, not a standard; terminals let users retheme these colors.

options._about: Three rendering options for the same mix. Each is valid alone or combined; none is the default.

rr-labelled.text: A cell whose background is the mixed color and whose text is the value (hex), drawn in black or white, chosen by the color's luminance.
behaviors: The label flips black/white at a luminance threshold, so a mid-gray mix changes label color near the boundary
#RRGGBB needs 7 columns, so the cell is at least that wide
The value sits on the color it names, so the readout and the swatch are read together
rr-labelled.principle: Print the value on the color it names.

rr-swatch.text: A full block (U+2588) in the mixed color as foreground, or spaces with the mixed color as background. No glyph shape competes with the color.
behaviors: A background-colored space shows the mix with no glyph at all, so it reads as pure color
Terminal cells are roughly twice as tall as wide, so two columns per swatch square up the fill
Swatch width and height trade off: a wider swatch is easier to judge, a taller one is easier to see from a distance
rr-swatch.principle: A fill shows the color itself; shading glyphs show only brightness.
signals: a flat block of one color

rr-ramp.text: Each cell takes one glyph from a ramp ordered sparse to dense. The mix's luminance picks the index, and the mixed color is the foreground, so hue survives the shading.
behaviors: A dark mix lands on dense glyphs such as @ or #; a light mix on sparse ones such as . or space
The luminance can be the encoded average or linear light; they differ mostly in mid-tones (see mm-linear-light)
On a dark background a dense glyph reads bright: index as-is for light backgrounds, reverse for dark ones
A short ramp gives coarse steps across a gradient; a longer one reads busier
rr-ramp.principle: Glyph density carries lightness; the color carries hue.
signals: glyph density steps as the ratio changes

tr-support-detection.text: No standard exists. COLORTERM=24bit or truecolor means 24-bit is safe; TERM ending in 256color means 256 is safe; otherwise assume basic ANSI.
signals: TERM=dumb or output not a TTY
behaviors: Output piped to a file should get no escapes; a CI log may claim dumb and still show color
tr-support-detection.principle: Detect the strongest supported mode and fall back in steps.

heading_path: Turning an Image into Gray Colors

tr-glyph-ramp.text: A shading ramp orders glyphs by ink density. Brightness indexes the ramp: a gray value maps to one character.
behaviors: Dense glyphs such as @ read darker than sparse ones such as . on a monospaced grid
signals: ramp runs from dense to sparse

tr-exemplar-pastel.text: A Rust command-line color tool with a mix command that blends two colors on the command line.
transfers: mix as a pure function from two colors and a fraction
does_not_transfer: no live key-driven rendering or ASCII picture

tr-exemplar-termpicker.text: An interactive terminal color picker; from a search snippet only, not fetched. It copies colors as hex, RGB, HSL, CMYK or ANSI truecolor.
does_not_transfer: picks colors rather than mixing them

tr-value-readouts.text: Tools show a color as hex, RGB, HSL or an ANSI code, and convert between formats on request.
signals: the same color in two formats side by side
behaviors: A mixed value shown in hex lets a reader check it against another tool

ansi16-table.text: Eight normal and eight bright colors; these are the Windows Terminal Campbell scheme values, and terminals vary. The purple key is the magenta slot.

rr-256-step.text: In 256-color mode a mix snaps to the nearest entry in the 6x6x6 color cube (levels 0, 95, 135, 175, 215, 255 per channel) or the 24-step gray ramp.
behaviors: Near-gray mixes may snap to the gray ramp, which is finer than the cube there
Channel levels are uneven, so the snap can shift hue more in some ranges than others
rr-256-step.principle: The 256 form is a palette lookup; the nearest entry is what gets shown.

rr-16-fallback.text: With only 16 colors, the mix snaps to the nearest named color: foreground 30 to 37 and 90 to 97, background 40 to 47 and 100 to 107. Ramp and swatch still work, with fewer hues.
behaviors: Mixes that differ slightly share one named color: the glyph ramp still steps, but the hue jumps
The shade a name shows depends on the terminal's theme, so the swatch may not match the hex
Bold may draw a named color brighter, which can shift the snapped result
rr-16-fallback.principle: When the screen can't show the exact color, keep the exact value in text.

rr-small-screen.term: minimum terminal size and small-screen behavior
rr-small-screen.text: A labelled cell needs at least 7 columns for its hex text, and a swatch runs 2 to 8 columns. The size floor that keeps both whole is a choice; the options sit in opt-min-size.
behaviors: A width near 7 columns keeps the hex text whole but leaves the swatch cramped
A floor of about 80 by 24 leaves room for swatch, label and readout together
With the lowest rows clipped instead of refused, a short window hides the readout first
rr-small-screen.principle: Size decides which parts of the picture survive; the floor only sets where that cut happens.
signals: readout cut off at small heights

rr-readout.term: color value readouts: hex, RGB, nearest ANSI name
rr-readout.text: A mix can be shown as #RRGGBB hex, as decimal R G B, or as the name of the nearest of the 16 ANSI colors. The name is an approximation; hex and RGB are the exact value.
behaviors: Hex and RGB show the exact mix; an ANSI name hides small changes between mixes
The nearest name depends on the distance metric: raw RGB distance and a perceptual one can pick different names for the same mix
Two different mixes can share one name, so a name alone reads as the same color twice
Hex with the name beside it shows the exact value and a rough name together
rr-readout.principle: A name alone merges distinct mixes; an exact value keeps each mix apart, and a name can sit beside it.
signals: same name for two different mixes
hex changes while the name stays put

mixing_model._about: The mixing model for a two-color mixer: four candidate models side by side, the readings of 'simple' that bear on the choice, and the ratio. Standard pairs are worked by hand from the standard formulas (rounded). The linear-light midpoint checks against the worked example in cp-linear-light.

options._about: options, not requirements: builder choices where the prompt is silent

opt-model-switch.term: one mix function with a model argument
opt-model-switch.text: mix(colors, weights, model) with model set to srgb, linear, multiply or lab, so the readings can be switched and compared without rewriting the program.

opt-two-readout.text: Show the channel-mean and linear-light results next to each other with their values, so the brightness difference is visible while mixing.

mm-lab.cost: about 40 to 60 lines for the sRGB, XYZ and Lab conversions and their inverses
mm-lab.text: Convert both colors to Lab, interpolate there, convert back. Lightness steps look even, but the midpoint is not a paint result.
behaviors: Red + blue gives about (202,0,136), a magenta-pink
Yellow + blue gives about (202,138,170), a salmon-pink, not green
Results outside sRGB clip back, which can shift the hue
mm-lab.principle: Lab interpolates perceived lightness and hue steadily; it does not model what happens when lights or pigments combine.
signals: pink or grey midpoint from yellow and blue
even steps in a lightness ramp

mm-ratio-n.text: A ratio t blends as (1 - t) * A + t * B in the chosen space. For N colors, use weights that sum to one; the multiply model needs a powered product instead.
behaviors: Ratio 0.5 is one step of many, not the default; checks at 0.25 and 0.75 show the model's shape
Changing the ratio should change the output color on every key press
mm-ratio-n.principle: The ratio is the control; the model decides what the in-between colors look like.
signals: output color changes with each step
weights that do not sum to one

tokens.t_steps: 0.1 to 0.9 in 0.1 steps, or 0.05 for a finer control

simple-readings.text: The size word bounds the mixing model. Each reading below is a different model choice, side by side. No reading is the default.

readings.in_practice: sum and halve each channel in one function; midpoints come out grey or dim
about 10 lines of sRGB decode and encode; brighter midpoints, same control code
one line that gives black for bright pairs; a usable paint model needs a chosen pigment set
about 40 to 60 lines of conversion; the conversions are the hard part, not the mix
signals: L, a and b names in the code

ev-red-blue-channel-mean.term: expected red and blue, channel mean
ev-red-blue-channel-mean.text: Expected output of the standard pair (red 255,0,0 and blue 0,0,255) under the channel mean model, at three ratios.

ev-red-blue-linear-light.term: expected red and blue, linear light
ev-red-blue-linear-light.text: Expected output of the standard pair (red 255,0,0 and blue 0,0,255) under the linear-light model, at three ratios. The t 0.5 value is 187.5 rounded to 188.

mm-subtractive.cost: channel multiply: 1 line; absorbance mix: about 6 lines and a floor; Kubelka-Munk: 15 to 25 lines plus reflectance data
mm-subtractive.text: Mix as pigments do: each input absorbs light, so the result gets darker. Three cost levels give very different results.
behaviors: Channel multiply gives (0,0,0) black for red + blue and for yellow + blue
A paint-like model gives green for yellow + blue and dark violet for red + blue (from paint behavior, not computed here)
Pure primaries have zero transmittance, so log-domain mixes need a floor such as 0.02
mm-subtractive.principle: Pigments multiply their absorption; a light model that multiplies channels turns bright pairs black.

tokens.reflectance_per_channel: 0.02 to 0.9, with a different pigment set giving a different green or violet

mm-average-srgb.text: Mix by taking the channel-wise mean of the gamma-encoded values. About one line of code, and the result matches the arithmetic a reader would do on the hex numbers.
behaviors: Yellow + blue gives (128,128,128), a mid grey
ev-red-blue-channel-mean holds the red and blue midpoints at three ratios
A two-color gradient dips dark in the middle
mm-average-srgb.principle: Averages the numbers as they are stored, so the output follows the hex arithmetic; it serves readers who want that predictability and the smallest code, and its midpoints are dimmer than the mix of light.
signals: grey midpoint from two bright colors
dark seam where two colors meet

mm-linear-light.cost: about 10 lines: sRGB decode, average, sRGB encode
mm-linear-light.text: Decode each sRGB channel to linear light, average there, then encode back. The midpoint comes out brighter than the channel mean.
behaviors: Red and blue keep the channel-mean hue at a lighter value (ev-red-blue-linear-light)
Yellow + blue gives (188,188,188), a lighter grey than the channel mean
A plain power of 2.2 is close to the piecewise sRGB curve but not exact
mm-linear-light.principle: Averages the light each channel stands for, so midpoints come out brighter than the channel mean; it serves readers who want the blend to match how light adds, and it costs about ten lines of sRGB conversion.
signals: brighter middle than the channel mean

tokens.gamma_exponent: 2.0 to 2.4, or the exact piecewise sRGB curve

interaction._about: Controls, state and feedback for the live mixer, with the failure cases a play check should cover. Facets and options, not a rulebook.

options._about: options, not requirements: builder choices where the prompt and evidence are silent

opt-step-size.text: Spread: 1 percent for fine tuning, 5 for quick sweeps, 10 for coarse moves; a shifted key for a larger step.

opt-history.text: Keep the last few mixes so a key recalls one; or keep only the current mix (the smaller reading).

opt-clamp-or-wrap.text: Three options for the ends: clamp (presses past 0 or 100 percent stop there); wrap (past 100 goes to 0, quick but easy to overshoot); bounce (the ratio turns back, so a held key sweeps up and down).

opt-start-colors.text: Starting pair, three options: a fixed pair (same each launch, easy to repeat), a random pair, or a pair chosen at launch. Whichever is used, the first screen shows both colors, the ratio, the swatch and the value.
behaviors: A fixed pair makes a play check repeatable; a random pair shows more of the range on each launch

opt-color-entry.text: Ways to set a color, side by side: typed hex (#RRGGBB), a typed name from the 16 ANSI names, an arrow-cycled list of presets, or a color given as a launch argument.
behaviors: Hex gives the exact color; a name or preset gives a coarse one
A bad hex entry prints a message and keeps the old color

opt-min-size.text: Size floors, side by side: 40 by 12 (swatch, hex and ratio, one line each), 60 by 18, 80 by 24 (the classic floor), 100 by 30 (room for both chips, the ratio bar and a large swatch).
behaviors: Below the floor, print one line that names the needed size and wait for a resize rather than draw a broken screen
Or reflow to a compact layout: swatch and value only, dropping the color chips

opt-key-map.text: Key sets, side by side: arrows (left and right move the ratio) or letters (a and d, or h and l), with + and - as a coarse step; q, Esc or Ctrl-C quit.
behaviors: Arrow keys need escape-sequence parsing; letter keys work in any terminal
A lone Esc waits briefly to tell it from an arrow's escape sequence
Ctrl-C exits and puts the terminal back out of raw mode

review_candidates._about: Play checks an output must pass, as questions with a concrete test each. Derived, so they carry from instead of prov.

ia-piped-output.text: When output is not a terminal, the program prints a plain value with no escape codes and no live loop.
properties: no raw key input without a TTY
behaviors: Piping the output to a file gives readable text, not escape sequences
ia-piped-output.principle: A terminal tool stays readable when its output is captured.
signals: ESC characters in a piped file
a prompt waiting on a closed input

ia-state.text: The engine holds the colors being mixed, one ratio per color, which color is selected, and the current mix.
behaviors: Changing the selection changes which ratio the keys move
The current mix can be recomputed from the colors and ratios on each read, or stored and updated on each change
tradeoffs: Recomputed: cannot drift, costs a little work per redraw
Stored: cheap to read, but a missed update shows a stale mix
ia-state.principle: The mix follows from the colors and ratios, so keep those as the one source; derive the mix or update it on every change.
signals: mix readout matches the ratios shown

ia-feedback.text: Every state change repaints the one screen: the swatch, the glyph rendering, the ratios and a readable value, all from the same stored state.
behaviors: A ratio change that does not repaint the swatch reads as broken
The swatch and the hex value come from the same stored color, so they cannot disagree
ia-feedback.principle: Every key shows its effect at once, on one screen.
signals: swatch and hex agree after a key
no stale frame after a change

ia-failure-cases.text: The program survives a terminal resize, exits promptly on its quit key or Ctrl-C, and rejects bad input without a crash.
behaviors: A resize triggers one full redraw at the new size
Quitting in raw mode without restoring the terminal leaves the shell garbled
A non-number entry prints a message and keeps the old ratio
ia-failure-cases.principle: Failure stays visible and recoverable; a traceback or a stuck terminal is the worst outcome.
signals: no traceback on resize or quit
typed text echoes normally after exit

ia-ratio-change.text: A key moves the ratio between two colors in fixed steps. The step size, the key set and the rule at the ends are options; the mix follows from the stored colors and ratio.
behaviors: Each press moves the ratio one step and the swatch changes at once
Holding a key repeats steps, so each step stays small enough to look smooth
ia-ratio-change.principle: A ratio is one number; keys move it and the chosen end rule decides what happens past 0 and 100 percent.
signals: ratio readout changes with each press
ratio stops, wraps or bounces at 0 and 100 percent

lexicon._about: Brain-dump vocabulary and associations around the prompt's words. Seed material at tier 3-4 (inferred, not fetched): it widens the work, it does not define the task. Quality readings are candidates; none is the default.

lx-color-mixing.text: Blending two or more colors into one, by light sums, pigment absorption, or a perceptual midpoint. People say blend, stir, cut with, tint, shade.
contribution: Albers, Interaction of Color: a color looks different next to another, so a mix is judged in context
Chevreul's simultaneous contrast: neighbours shift each other's apparent hue
Kubelka-Munk: a physical model of paint absorption and scattering, deeper than a simple average
Munsell notation: a perceptual grid of hue, value and chroma for naming a mix
theatre gels (Lee filters): stacked gels subtract light, a real-world subtractive mix
Goethe's colour theory: colour as perception and contrast, an odd but durable lineage

lx-ascii.text: Pictures drawn with printable characters, where glyph density, shape or a fixed grid stands for brightness or colour.
contribution: AAlib and libcaca: libraries that map images to characters, with colour in libcaca
BBS and ANSI art: coloured text cells as a whole medium
Joan G. Stark: hand-built ASCII pictures that use character shape, not only density
demoscene text mode: colour-cycled characters as a graphic effect
Figlet: large letters built from text, a label rather than a picture

lx-interactive.text: A program that responds to each input while it runs, so the user adjusts a value and sees the result change.
contribution: Shneiderman: direct manipulation, the object changes as you act on it
Bret Victor's essays: see the effect of a change as you make it
curses and TUI tools (htop, k9s): redraw one screen on each key
immediate mode GUI (Dear ImGui): redraw each frame from state, no widget tree
a mixing desk fader: a ratio you move by feel, in steps

lx-simple.text: A size word for the build: small scope and few parts. It bounds the work, it does not narrow what is shown.
contribution: Dieter Rams, less but better: each element earns its place
Tufte's data-ink ratio: remove ink that carries no data
Forth one-screen programs: a whole tool on one page of code
Unix small tools: one job, composable through text

q-simple.text: The size word can be read three ways here; each sets a different bound on the build.

readings.reading: one screen of state and a few keys
readings.in_practice: One file, one loop, two colors and one ratio; the mix, its value and the keys fit on one screen.
readings.exemplar: two color inputs, one ratio key, one swatch, hex readout

readings.in_practice: A line-based tool: mix two colors at a given ratio, print the value, repeat. No live redraw.

readings.reading: a single function with a test-friendly call
readings.in_practice: A pure function from two colors and a ratio to one color; a thin interface wraps it so tests call it directly.
signals: returns a value, not a print
readings.exemplar: mix(color_a, color_b, ratio) returns one color

q-ascii.text: The output is ASCII, and the characters can carry the picture three ways.

readings.in_practice: A sparse-to-dense ramp of characters across the full range, so each brightness step shows as a glyph change.
Each cell is a full block or spaces on a background set to the mix; the color fills the cell.
readings.exemplar: a 10 by 4 cell filled with the mixed color

readings.in_practice: Each cell prints its hex or name over the mix in a contrasting color, so value and color sit together.
readings.exemplar: cell shows '#7f3fbf' in white or black, whichever contrasts

q-interactive.text: The user acts while it runs. Three readings differ in how quickly the screen answers a key.

readings.in_practice: Every key that changes the ratio redraws the swatch, the glyphs and the readout within one frame, with no Enter needed.
readings.exemplar: left and right arrows move the ratio, swatch repaints each press

readings.reading: update on Enter after a typed command
readings.in_practice: The user types a mix command and presses Enter; the screen updates once per command.

readings.reading: a slider-like ratio that moves in steps
readings.in_practice: The ratio is a bar with fixed steps; holding a key sweeps it, and the mix updates at each step, so the change is always discrete and visible.
readings.exemplar: a 20-step bar from colour A to colour B

lx-taxonomy-technical.term: colour mixing vocabulary: technical and perceptual
lx-taxonomy-technical.text: Register of the mixing model itself. Light, paint and perceptual senses are all meant until the build picks one.
signals: muddy midpoint darker than both ends

lx-taxonomy-objects.term: colour mixing vocabulary: objects, cells and readouts
lx-taxonomy-objects.text: Nouns and verbs a terminal mixer uses. Swatch and ramp are the picture; hex and ANSI name are the readout.
signals: swatch and value agree after a key
